prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Sometimes, mystified by the behaviorof one of my sons, my wife will point out if it’s age-appropriate, making me wonder why I still shout at ballplayers on tv and argue with the dead. Last week, my oldest son,with a wild pitch, turned my left ankle into an eggplant. I didn’t yell at the doctors who refused my insurance, or get angry with a friend who told me to soak it in bourbon and garlic. No,I read Montaigne who said self-revelation is the purpose of discourse, which, in his day, meant knowing whether to be flattered if a friend didn’t use a food-taster, or amused if a witch cast a spell of weeping on an in-law. Blaise Monluc, the king’s lieutenant general during the civil wars, Montaigne says,threw so many hanged Protestantsdown a well you could reach in and touch the top one’s head. Yes,Monluc, who was fond of saying “When the scaffolds are full, use trees,” knew what was appropriate. On occasion I’ll run into a lobbyto avoid greeting a friend, not because my mind vanishes and I can’t remember his name, which is true, but because I must flee what is darkest in me. In other words, when evicted from a strange lobby into a stranger street, where every scaffold is full and bodies dangle in the long blue sorrow of the afternoon, without context, explanation, or sympathy,it’s good to know, even momentarily, how to live, among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Sometimes, Last, Montaigne

outputs.L1: Sometimes, mystified by the behavior of one of my sons, my wife will point out that it is age-appropriate, leaving me to wonder why I still shout at ballplayers on TV and argue with the dead. Last week, my oldest son, with a wild pitch, turned my left ankle into an eggplant. I didn’t yell at the doctors who refused my insurance, or grow angry with a friend who told me to soak it in bourbon and garlic. No, I read Montaigne, who said self-revelation is the purpose of discourse—which, in his day, meant knowing whether to be flattered if a friend didn’t use a food-taster, or amused if a witch cast a spell of weeping on an in-law. Blaise Monluc, the king’s lieutenant general during the civil wars, Montaigne says, threw so many hanged Protestants down a well that you could reach in and touch the top one’s head. Yes, Monluc, who was fond of saying, “When the scaffolds are full, use trees,” knew what was appropriate. On occasion, I’ll run into a lobby to avoid greeting a friend—not because my mind vanishes and I can’t remember his name, which is true, but because I must flee what is darkest in me. In other words, when evicted from a strange lobby into a stranger street, where every scaffold is full and bodies dangle in the long blue sorrow of the afternoon, without context, explanation, or sympathy, it is good to know, even momentarily, how to live among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.
outputs.L2:
At times, when one of my sons acts in some baffling way, my wife will remark on whether the behavior suits his age, which makes me ask myself why I continue to yell at athletes on television and quarrel with people who are dead. A week ago, my eldest boy, by means of a wayward pitch, made my left ankle swell and purple like an eggplant. I did not berate the doctors who would not accept my insurance, nor did I take offense at the friend who advised me to bathe it in bourbon and garlic. Instead, I turned to Montaigne, who wrote that the aim of conversation is to disclose the self—an idea that, in his era, involved understanding whether one should feel honored when a friend dispensed with a food-taster, or merely entertained when a witch placed a crying curse on a relative by marriage. Montaigne also tells us that Blaise Monluc, the king’s lieutenant general in the civil wars, had so many executed Protestants thrown into a well that a person could reach down and touch the head of the uppermost corpse. Indeed, Monluc—the man who liked to say, “When the scaffolds are full, use trees”—understood propriety.

Now and then, I will duck into a lobby to avoid saying hello to a friend. This is not only because my memory blanks and I cannot call up his name, though that is also the case, but because I feel compelled to escape the worst part of myself. Put another way: when one is expelled from an unfamiliar lobby onto an even more unfamiliar street, where every scaffold has been filled and bodies hang in the long blue grief of the afternoon, with no context, no explanation, and no pity, it helps to understand, if only for an instant, how to go on living among those who are relevant, fervent, and bewildered.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the idea of age-appropriate behavior, questioning what it means to act in a way that properly corresponds to one’s stage of life. He recognizes that maturity does not necessarily free a person from irrational habits, sudden reactions, or private absurdities. Even as an adult—and perhaps especially as a parent—he finds himself subject to impulses that do not fit neatly with ideals of wisdom, composure, or self-control. This awareness gives the reflection a self-critical tone: he is not simply judging others for their foolishness but examining his own.

This becomes clear when his son injures his ankle. The situation might easily provoke frustration, panic, or anger, especially if the injury seems inconvenient or avoidable. Instead, the speaker responds by turning to Montaigne. Rather than treating the accident as merely a domestic irritation, he uses it as an occasion for thought. Montaigne offers him a way to step back from immediate emotion and consider human behavior with greater patience and perspective. The injury becomes less a crisis than a moment in which the speaker tests his own capacity for judgment.

Montaigne’s belief that discourse is a form of self-revelation shapes the speaker’s meditation. To speak, write, or reason about the world is also to disclose oneself: one’s fears, assumptions, vanities, and limitations appear in the very act of commentary. The speaker’s reflections on age, parenting, anger, and confusion therefore become more than abstract observations. They reveal his own character. Like Montaigne, he understands thinking as a process that exposes the thinker, not as a detached performance of certainty.

The text then broadens its scope by contrasting ordinary personal confusion with the far darker disorder of history. The speaker’s own irrational habits and family frustrations are set beside the brutality of Blaise Monluc during the French civil wars. Monluc’s violence represents a world in which judgment has not merely faltered but collapsed into cruelty. This historical example reminds the speaker that human beings are capable not only of minor foolishness but of terrifying moral failure. The comparison gives weight to the meditation, moving it beyond private embarrassment toward a larger concern with the destructive possibilities of human conduct.

In the end, the speaker suggests that life unfolds within a chaotic and morally troubling world, one in which people often fail to understand themselves or act well toward others. Yet this does not make reflection useless. On the contrary, even brief moments of clarity matter. If one can, for a moment, understand how to live—with restraint, humility, patience, or compassion—that moment has value. The speaker does not claim to possess lasting wisdom. Instead, he finds significance in temporary insight, in the fragile but meaningful effort to become more aware of how one should act.
outputs.L4:
I recently found myself wondering, not for the first time, how old a person is supposed to be before he stops behaving foolishly. The question did not arise in some grand moral crisis, or after a dramatic betrayal, or in the shadow of public disgrace. It came, more humiliatingly, from an ankle injury.

I had hurt myself in a way that was both painful and ridiculous, the kind of accident that makes one angry not only at the body but at the story that must later be told about it. There are injuries that invite sympathy: a fall on ice, a sports accident, a collision, some noble overextension. Mine felt like evidence. Evidence of clumsiness, impatience, vanity, or some combination of all three. The pain was real enough, but what troubled me more was the embarrassment attached to it. I was old enough, I thought, to know better. But “old enough” is a strange phrase. Old enough for what? To move carefully? To accept limits? To stop wanting to appear uninjured, unbothered, young?

The ankle became, absurdly, a moral object. I was angry at it, then angry at myself for being angry at it. I avoided people because I did not want to explain what had happened. I avoided mirrors because they seemed to confirm the ungainliness I felt. I avoided the very thought of the incident because it led too quickly into a swamp of self-judgment. A trivial injury exposed a familiar confusion: the gap between the person one thinks one has become and the person who still reacts with pettiness, shame, and rage.

This is where Montaigne becomes useful. He is useful not because he offers a cure for embarrassment, but because he refuses to pretend that human beings are more coherent than they are. In the *Essays*, he makes himself the subject, but not in the modern sense of self-promotion or confession for applause. He observes himself as one might observe weather: changeable, contradictory, sometimes beautiful, often inconvenient. He does not reveal himself in order to become exemplary. He reveals himself because the self, honestly examined, is already strange enough to be worth studying.

Montaigne’s greatness lies partly in his willingness to include what other writers might hide. He writes of fear, digestion, friendship, cowardice, habit, education, death, and the instability of judgment. He does not present wisdom as a permanent possession. Wisdom, in him, is intermittent. It flickers. It appears in a sentence and disappears in the next appetite, the next prejudice, the next bodily complaint. Reading him, one has the comforting sense that inconsistency is not an exception to human life but one of its basic conditions.

This does not excuse everything. To say that people are confused is not to say that cruelty is harmless, or that anger is merely charming, or that weakness absolves us. Montaigne knew this too. His age was not gentle. Behind the humane intelligence of the *Essays* lies a Europe disfigured by religious violence, torture, massacre, and fanaticism. His reflections on the self are never entirely separate from the brutality of history. The private mind and the public world are entangled. A person who cannot examine his own anger may become, under the right conditions, an instrument of something much worse than embarrassment.

That is the darker implication. The same human being who sulks over a sprained ankle belongs to the species that invents racks, burnings, purges, camps, and righteous slogans for murder. The absurd and the monstrous are not identical, but they are not wholly unrelated either. Both begin in the unstable creature that we are: proud, frightened, needy, imaginative, easily humiliated, eager to justify ourselves. Moral darkness is not always dramatic at first. Sometimes it begins as avoidance, as the refusal to look directly at what one has done or felt. Sometimes it begins with the small lie that one’s anger is pure.

This is why self-examination matters, though it cannot save us once and for all. To look inward honestly is not to become innocent. It is to become less surprised by one’s own capacity for evasion. It is to notice the quick movement by which embarrassment turns into blame, pain into resentment, uncertainty into contempt. Such noticing may not make us good, but it can interrupt us. It can create a pause between impulse and action. In that pause, if we are lucky, there is room for judgment.

Reading can create a similar pause. A book does not abolish confusion, but it can give confusion a shape. Montaigne, especially, offers the relief of company without simplification. He does not stand above the reader like a judge. He sits nearby, equally implicated, speaking across centuries in a tone at once intimate and unsparing. His self-revelation gives permission for our own, but it also raises the standard: if we are to speak about ourselves, we should try not to lie.

The ankle healed, as ankles usually do. The embarrassment lasted longer, because embarrassment is less a wound than a story, and stories can be rehearsed long after the body has recovered. Yet even that humiliation became less useless when I could see it as part of a larger pattern. I had wanted to appear composed. I was not composed. I had wanted to be beyond childish anger. I was not beyond it. I had wanted age to mean immunity from foolishness. It does not.

Perhaps maturity is not the disappearance of such reactions, but the ability to recognize them sooner and obey them less. Perhaps age-appropriate behavior is not a fixed code but a continuing negotiation with one’s own absurdity. We do not become wise by ceasing to be ridiculous. We become wiser, if at all, by learning how ridiculousness feels from the inside and by refusing to let shame harden into cruelty.

There is no grand consolation here. History remains brutal. Human beings remain evasive. Pain and vanity continue to make fools of us. But for brief moments, reading and reflection can orient us. They can remind us that confusion is not the same as helplessness, that anger need not be sovereign, that moral attention begins in small acts of honesty. Montaigne does not tell us exactly how to live. He does something more fragile and perhaps more useful: he shows a person trying to find out.

That effort may be the best we have. Amid cruelty, absurdity, and confusion, we examine what we can: a memory, a reaction, a sentence, a limp. We look at the world’s darkness and at our own smaller shadows, not because looking is enough, but because not looking is worse. For a little while, the act of attention steadies us. It gives us, however briefly, a sense of where we are and how we might proceed.
outputs.L5:
Sometimes, the most lasting wisdom comes from those who refused to pretend they had all the answers. Michel de Montaigne, the French Renaissance writer, built his essays around uncertainty, observation, and honest self-questioning. Rather than presenting himself as a final authority, he explored his thoughts as they changed, admitting contradiction and doubt.

At last, this may be why Montaigne still feels modern. He understood that human beings are inconsistent, shaped by habit, mood, fear, and curiosity. His famous question, “What do I know?” invites us to pause before judging others too quickly or trusting our own opinions too completely.

Sometimes we search for fixed truths, but Montaigne reminds us that reflection itself has value. The last word is not always certainty; sometimes it is humility.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, lyrical personal essay in the style of a contemporary American prose poem, beginning with a father reflecting on age-appropriate behavior and ending with a meditation on how to live among “the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.”
counterfactuals.output:
My father used to say there was such a thing as age-appropriate behavior, and then he would look down at his own hands as if they had been caught doing something childish: worrying a napkin into lint, drumming the table during grace, reaching for another roll not out of hunger but out of the old animal wish to be comforted by warmth. He believed, or wanted us to believe, that life was a series of rooms one entered properly dressed: childhood with its noise and jammed fingers, adolescence with its fragrant shame, adulthood with its bills and weather, old age with its quiet bowl of pills. But he laughed too loudly at funerals, cried during commercials in which a dog found its way home, bought himself a red bicycle after his second surgery and rode it at dusk through the neighborhood, knees shining like doorknobs, while the children called after him, Mister, Mister, do a wheelie.

I have inherited his confusion, which may be another word for tenderness. I am old enough now to know better and young enough, apparently, not to. I still want to be forgiven for the wrong things. I still mistake intensity for truth. I still keep certain sorrows in a drawer with dead batteries, foreign coins, keys to apartments I no longer live in, as though someday a door will present itself and I will be ready, jangling and official. The body goes on being embarrassing in its loyalty: it wants sugar, touch, sleep, applause, the particular blue of a swimming pool in July. Meanwhile the mind, that municipal clerk, keeps stamping forms: expired, insufficient, pending review.

There were years I tried to become a person with clean edges. I answered emails promptly. I learned the names of cheeses. I said, Let’s circle back, and felt part of my soul step politely into traffic. I mistook composure for wisdom, distance for dignity. At dinner parties I praised restraint while my heart, under the table, gnawed through its leash. What I wanted was never reasonable. I wanted the dead to write. I wanted the living to stop leaving. I wanted my father to tell me that age was a rumor, that no one graduates from longing, that every decade is only a different weather system moving through the same field.

When he became ill, the rooms collapsed into each other. He was a boy again, furious at soup, suspicious of spoons, delighted by orange sherbet. I was the parent and not the parent, the child and not the child, standing beside his bed while the machines made their small arguments with silence. He asked once if he had behaved. The question entered me like a winter bird. Behaved for whom? For the nurses, the gods, the invisible committee of adulthood? I told him yes, because mercy is sometimes a lie with its sleeves rolled up. He smiled, relieved, and fell asleep with his mouth slightly open, as if still expecting snow.

After he died, I found the bicycle in the garage, its tires collapsed, its red frame dusty but extravagant, a little flame leaned against a wall of paint cans and rakes. I thought of all the ways we are asked to dim ourselves in order to be legible. Be mature. Be realistic. Be strategic. Be healed. But grief is not strategic. Desire is not realistic. Joy appears in the wrong clothes, at the wrong hour, asking to borrow the car. And the soul, if there is one, is never age-appropriate. It is a child with an ancient face, an old man skipping stones, a woman dancing alone in the kitchen after terrible news, because the song has come on and the body, poor faithful instrument, remembers what the mind has forbidden.

So I have begun to distrust the calendar’s authority. I respect appointments, but not verdicts. I pay what I can, answer what I must, apologize when the harm is mine. Still, I leave room for the ridiculous: the bright bicycle, the second piece of cake, the letter written too late, the hand held too long, the sudden confession beside the avocados. I am trying to live less like a résumé and more like a field after rain: receptive, muddy, temporary, full of evidence that something has passed through and something else is coming.

If age teaches anything, perhaps it is not propriety but proportion: how small the self is, how large its hunger; how brief the quarrel, how durable the ache; how every person is carrying a weather of which they are only partly the author. My father wanted order, but what he gave me was permission: to be mixed, unfinished, extravagant with feeling; to let the rooms of life open into each other; to stand at the table of years with my napkin shredded, my hands unhidden, my heart neither young nor old but stubbornly awake, learning, at last, how to live among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-paragraph literary essay that moves associatively from family life and a minor injury to Montaigne, Blaise de Monluc, religious violence, social avoidance, and a final philosophical reflection on context and sympathy.
counterfactuals.output: At dinner the child’s bandaged finger, nicked by a kitchen knife while helping with carrots, becomes the small red hinge on which the household turns: one parent soothing, another scolding too quickly from fear, siblings staring with the grave curiosity reserved for blood and weather, and the whole domestic scene acquiring that disproportionate intensity by which family life converts trifles into moral instruction. Montaigne would have recognized the comedy and tenderness of it, the way the body interrupts our pretensions and restores us to scale; in his essays, a fall from a horse, a kidney stone, a memory lapse, or a servant’s error can widen into a meditation on custom, cruelty, fear, and the instability of judgment. He knew, too, that a wound is never merely a wound once men begin to narrate it, for his century turned torn flesh into doctrine and doctrine into torn flesh: Blaise de Monluc, that hard old captain of the French Wars of Religion, could describe executions and reprisals with the brisk authority of one who believed severity was a form of order, while Montaigne, living amid the same convulsions, learned to distrust the intoxications of certainty. Between them lies the difference between the hand that tightens on the sword and the mind that hesitates over a sentence, yet both belong to a world in which neighbors crossed streets to avoid one another, households concealed opinions, and ordinary sociability was poisoned by the suspicion that a greeting, a meal, even a silence might disclose allegiance. Such avoidance has its modest descendants: the relative not invited because politics will spoil the holiday, the friend unanswered because grief is awkward, the injured child briefly resented for disturbing the evening’s fragile peace. We like to think ourselves humane in the abstract, but sympathy depends on nearness, timing, and the story we have already begun telling about the other person; context does not excuse violence or coldness, but it explains how easily the heart narrows when fear supplies the frame. To understand this is not to pardon Monluc, nor to sentimentalize Montaigne, nor even to absolve the parent who snaps before comforting; it is to see that judgment without context becomes vanity, while context without judgment becomes surrender, and that sympathy—our best, most difficult art—begins in holding both together, as one holds a wounded finger under running water: firmly, patiently, and with attention to the pain that is not one’s own.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal memoir fragment narrated by a father whose son injures his ankle, who then reads Montaigne and connects the incident to historical cruelty, friendship, embarrassment, and the problem of knowing what behavior is appropriate.
counterfactuals.output:
When my son twisted his ankle, the whole afternoon bent with it.

We had been walking beside the municipal pond, that shallow green eye where ducks appeared to be thinking badly of us. He was twelve, or perhaps he was younger in the way children become younger when they are hurt. One moment he was leaping from the curb with the ceremonial foolishness of a boy proving gravity had no jurisdiction over him; the next he sat on the path, both hands around his ankle, his face pale with an expression I recognized but could not name. Pain is often less frightening than its etiquette. Should he cry? Should I touch him? Should I say, “It’s all right,” when plainly it was not? A father is expected to know the proper distance between alarm and reassurance, but I have never been furnished with that measuring instrument.

The ducks came nearer. One of them, a white domestic duck with an orange bill the color of a courtroom stamp, stared at me as if awaiting testimony.

I carried my son to the car. He was heavier than I expected, and I was embarrassed by this fact—as if his weight were a private accusation, proof that I had not been paying attention while he became a body. His arms clasped my neck. I felt his breath in my ear, damp and indignant. In the parking lot, a woman loading groceries paused to watch us. I smiled at her, absurdly, as though carrying an injured child were a public performance and I wished to assure the audience that no serious mistake had been made.

At home, after ice, elevation, an elastic bandage, and a series of paternal pronouncements copied from television doctors, he fell asleep on the sofa. His foot lay on a pillow like a pale animal with a blue mouth. I sat beside him and opened Montaigne.

It was the essay on cruelty, though in my memory all of Montaigne is one essay, a man pacing a tower while history gnaws the stairs below him. He wrote of punishments, of torture, of the Roman games, of how easily human beings become accustomed to spectacles of suffering. He seemed offended not only by cruelty itself but by the neatness with which people justify it, the way they put moral napkins on the table before carving one another. I read while my son slept, his ankle swelling quietly, the small domestic version of catastrophe.

Outside the window the evening had turned the color of old pewter. The maple tree leaned toward the house. Its branches looked like hands that had forgotten whether they meant to bless or strangle.

I thought of all the ankles broken in history and not bandaged. Prisoners marched until their feet opened. Children in wars who learned the geometry of rubble before they learned fractions. Men displayed on wheels. Women accused, examined, burned, watched by neighbors who must have known how to behave in public. There is a horror in this: that cruelty is so often accompanied by manners. Someone holds the cloak. Someone looks away at the correct moment. Someone says, “These are the times,” and sleeps well.

My son murmured in his dream and shifted. I reached out to adjust the ice pack, then hesitated. I did not want to wake him. I did not want to fail him by caution. The problem of conduct opened before me like an encyclopedia written in a language I had almost learned.

Montaigne, at least, admits confusion. He does not arrive polished and armed with certainties; he arrives in his slippers, scratching his head. He is humane partly because he is embarrassed. Reading him, I felt the old shame of being a person among persons: how often I had laughed too loudly at another man’s misfortune, how often I had mistaken discomfort for wit, how often I had remained silent because I could not determine whether speech would be noble or merely theatrical.

Friendship, Montaigne suggested elsewhere, was a mystery so complete that explanation damaged it. “Because it was he, because it was I.” I closed the book on my finger and looked at my son. Parenthood is not friendship, not exactly; it is more tyrannical, more bodily, less chosen. Yet there are moments when one’s child appears not as an extension of oneself, nor as a responsibility, but as a stranger entrusted to one’s temporary care by a negligent universe. Because it was he, because it was I: this seemed suddenly less like a definition of friendship than the only possible answer to any cry for help.

In the kitchen, the refrigerator began its nightly groan. The sound became, in my tiredness, the creaking of a medieval rack. The elastic bandage on my son’s ankle unrolled in my imagination into a road, then into a banner, then into the pale intestine of history itself, winding through courts and battlefields and schoolyards. Everywhere, people were deciding what was appropriate. How much pain to acknowledge. How much to inflict. Whether to intervene. Whether to smile at strangers in parking lots. Whether to say, “Be brave,” to someone who had not asked for bravery.

When my son woke, he looked at me with the irritated dignity of the recently injured.

“Is it broken?” he asked.

“I don’t think so,” I said.

“You don’t know.”

“No,” I admitted. “I don’t know.”

This pleased him more than my earlier assurances. He sat up slightly, winced, and then, seeing the Montaigne in my lap, asked what I was reading.

“A man trying to figure out how to live,” I said.

“Does he?”

“No. But he’s good company.”

My son considered this. Then he asked for toast.

I made it carefully, as if toast were an ethical act. The butter tore small golden holes in the bread. I brought it to him on a plate, and he ate with the solemn appetite of the recovering. Crumbs fell onto his shirt. I did not brush them away.

For once, I knew enough not to.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an erudite, darkly comic prose piece that mixes domestic absurdity, baseball, insurance problems, folk remedies, Montaigne’s Essays, French civil wars, and the narrator’s fear of his own inner darkness.
counterfactuals.output:
By the time the raccoon fell through the kitchen ceiling, my wife and I had already agreed that the house was not so much a dwelling as a philosophical proposition advanced by a malicious Cartesian. It leaked, therefore it was. The south wall sighed in damp weather. The dishwasher, though empty, made a nightly noise like a regiment dragging cannon through Burgundy. In the pantry, the flour had acquired a baroque interior life. We were, in short, homeowners, which is to say minor officials in a bureaucracy of rot.

The raccoon landed in the fruit bowl, displacing three pears and a commemorative baseball signed—allegedly—by a middle reliever for the 1998 Montreal Expos. It blinked at us with the solemnity of a papal legate. My wife, who in crises becomes brisk and Roman, said, “Don’t move.” I, who in crises become literary and useless, thought of Montaigne.

“What do I know?” I whispered.

“You know the number for animal control,” she said.

This was true, though only in the way one knows the phone number of one’s childhood dentist: as a relic of a civilization that has collapsed. Animal control was closed for the evening due to “staffing limitations.” Our insurance company’s emergency line placed me on hold beneath a cheerful marimba arrangement of “Take Me Out to the Ball Game,” which, after twenty-seven minutes, began to seem less like music than a legal argument against hope.

The raccoon, meanwhile, ate a pear.

I have never trusted pears. They ripen in secrecy and die at noon.

Our insurer, when finally reached, wanted to know whether the raccoon had entered through “storm-related damage, preexisting structural vulnerability, or an act of God.” I asked if those categories were mutually exclusive. The representative, whose name was Kaylee and whose voice was smooth with the refrigerated kindness of a modern corporation, said she was not authorized to interpret divinity.

“Suppose,” I said, “God acts through a preexisting structural vulnerability.”

There was a pause, during which I imagined Kaylee consulting a laminated chart: hail, yes; flood, no; vermin, maybe; wrath, deductible applies.

“Sir,” she said, “was the raccoon deceased upon entry?”

“No,” I said. “It appears vigorous. Almost Huguenot.”

My wife looked at me sharply. She dislikes it when I bring the French Wars of Religion into practical affairs, though I maintain they are nearly always relevant. What is marriage, after all, if not a fragile Edict of Nantes negotiated between rival doctrines concerning laundry, thermostats, and the proper loading of knives? What is a family but a besieged La Rochelle, eating its own shoe leather while cardinals in red watch from expensive chairs?

The raccoon climbed onto the counter and knocked over the bottle of elderberry tincture my mother had mailed us “for immunity, inflammation, and spiritual mildew.” My mother believes in doctors, but only as a last resort, after garlic poultices, mustard plasters, salt baths, apple-cider vinegar, cod liver oil, and the laying-on of hands by women named Barb. When I was eleven and had scarlet fever, she rubbed my chest with goose grease and read aloud from the Farmer’s Almanac. I survived, which she took as evidence.

“Maybe the elderberry will calm him,” my wife said.

“He’s a wild animal,” I said.

“So are you after the Mets lose.”

The Mets had lost that afternoon in a manner at once operatic and municipal. A three-run lead had gone out into the seventh inning dressed like a respectable uncle and returned in the ninth as a police report. Our closer, a man paid more annually than the assessed value of our zip code, had thrown twelve consecutive balls. The announcer used the word “uncharacteristic,” though anyone with a historical imagination could see in it the St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre: confusion at the palace, bells in the night, blood in the streets, Protestants at the window, Catholics on first and third with nobody out.

Montaigne lived through that slaughtering century with his library tower, his kidney stones, his cat, his humane skepticism. While zealots sharpened doctrine into knives, he sat among beams inscribed with Latin and Greek, asking whether any man was wise enough to kill another for an abstraction. I admire him because he made uncertainty sturdy. He did not turn doubt into paralysis, as I do, nor into cynicism, as the internet has done, but into a chair by the fire.

Yet even Montaigne had servants to deal with the wildlife.

The raccoon sneezed.

My wife said, “Do raccoons carry plague?”

“Everyone carries something,” I said.

This, I admit, was not helpful.

Kaylee returned from her consultation and informed me that our policy did not cover “intrusion by undomesticated mammals unless consequent to a covered peril.” I said the peril was obvious: the mammal was in the kitchen. She said the peril must precede the mammal. I told her causality itself had become porous since the ceiling opened. She said she could open a claim but could not guarantee reimbursement. I asked whether despair was itemized separately or bundled with remediation. She thanked me for being a valued customer.

While I argued, my wife armed herself with a broom, a laundry basket, and the unearned confidence of the Midwestern Protestant. She had grown up in a town where people put pie on windowsills without irony and treated tornadoes as weather with opinions. She advanced on the raccoon. The raccoon advanced on the peanut butter.

“Don’t antagonize him,” I said.

“I’m not antagonizing him. I’m redirecting him.”

“That’s what Richelieu said.”

“Get the door.”

I opened the back door onto the yard, where the porch light illuminated our crabgrass, the collapsed tomato cages, and the child’s batting tee I had bought in a fit of paternal optimism though we have no children. I sometimes purchase objects intended for a better, more wholesome version of myself: running shoes, blank notebooks, a mandoline slicer, a biography of Erasmus, the batting tee. The better man never arrives. The objects remain, small monuments to an empire of intention.

My wife lifted the broom.

The raccoon hissed.

In that sound I heard not merely animal displeasure but the old black note beneath things: the unadmitted appetite, the cellar door in the skull, the little tyrant in me who would, under sufficient historical pressure, denounce neighbors, hoard flour, cheer executions, enjoy the fire. It is easy to imagine oneself Montaigne, temperate among fanatics, stroking one’s cat while composing essays on cannibals and custom. It is harder, late at night with damp insulation on your floor and insurance denying metaphysics, to know whether one’s soul contains more of the essayist or the mob.

This is my fear: not that I am wicked in some grand, operatic way, but that I am ordinary enough for wickedness to use. That my civility is only good plumbing. That my tolerance depends on coffee, ibuprofen, stable currency, and a bullpen that can retire the side. Remove these, add hunger, chanting, a persuasive man on horseback, and who knows? Perhaps I too would find a doctrine to excuse the pleasure of breaking glass.

“Are you brooding?” my wife said.

“Yes.”

“Stop. He’s under the table.”

The raccoon had taken refuge beneath the kitchen table, where among the chair legs it resembled a masked magistrate hiding from revolution. My wife crouched with the laundry basket. I stood by the door holding a jar of Vicks VapoRub, because at some point, without informing my reason, my hand had reached for a folk remedy. My grandmother swore Vicks cured coughs, bee stings, loneliness, warts, communism, and the vague peril of being indoors in March. She applied it to the soles of our feet and covered them with socks, an act I have never seen defended in peer-reviewed literature but which had the gravity of sacrament.

“What are you going to do with that?” my wife asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Then do it quietly.”

I unscrewed the lid. The kitchen filled with eucalyptus, menthol, and ancestral credulity. The raccoon sniffed, recoiled, and bolted—not toward the open door, naturally, but into the living room, where it scrambled over the sofa, across the coffee table, and onto the shelf containing my Everyman edition of Montaigne’s Essays. There it paused, one paw on “Of Experience,” and stared at me with bright, prosecutorial eyes.

Reader, I felt judged.

Not by the raccoon alone. By Montaigne, by my mother’s goose grease, by the dead Expos, by the unpaid claim adjusters of history. By all those men in the sixteenth century who believed themselves instruments of God while behaving like raccoons in a pantry. By my own secret self, crouched under the table, striped and hungry, waiting for the ceiling to give way.

Then the animal defecated on the rug.

This, too, was philosophy.

At last, by means too humiliating to report fully, involving a bath towel, a saucepan, two contradictory YouTube videos, and my wife’s command voice—“Outside, you little cardinal!”—we expelled the beast into the yard. It vanished beneath the hydrangeas with the offended dignity of a statesman resigning under scandal.

The house was silent except for the steady drip from the ceiling into the fruit bowl.

My wife and I stood amid insulation, pear pulp, Vicks fumes, and the faint ecclesiastical stink of raccoon. The baseball had rolled under the radiator. I retrieved it and wiped it with a dishcloth. The signature, never very convincing, had blurred into an illegible blue heresy.

“Do you think insurance will pay?” she asked.

“No,” I said.

“Do you think the ceiling will collapse again?”

“Yes.”

“Do you think there are more raccoons?”

I looked at the hole above us, black as doctrine.

“Almost certainly.”

She sighed and leaned her head against my shoulder. There are moments in marriage when despair becomes so complete it is indistinguishable from comfort. Outside, something rustled in the shrubs. Inside, Montaigne lay open on the floor, his pages damp but legible. I picked up the book and read the first sentence my eye found: “We are, I know not how, double in ourselves.”

“Listen to this,” I said.

“No,” my wife said. “Get a bucket.”

So I got a bucket.

And because civilization consists largely of doing the obvious thing after exhausting the ornamental alternatives, I placed it beneath the leak. Then I washed my hands, spread Vicks on my wrists for no medical reason whatsoever, and sat at the kitchen table beneath the wounded ceiling, keeping watch like a minor lord in a ruined province, uncertain whether the darkness above me belonged to the attic, to history, or to myself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a compact nonfiction-style monologue with long sentences and ironic turns, where the narrator compares shouting at TV athletes and avoiding acquaintances with Montaigne’s examples of manners, violence, and self-revelation.
counterfactuals.output:
I have learned, in the humane laboratory of the living room, that a man may denounce a goalkeeper for hesitation while hesitating three days to answer a harmless message from an acquaintance, and if Montaigne could find in the way we greet, eat, bow, lie, flinch, boast, and endure pain a whole map of the soul, then surely there is some small essay to be made from the citizen who roars “shoot” at a millionaire athlete on television and then crosses the street to avoid a colleague whose only known crime is conversational persistence.  

Montaigne liked to notice that manners are not trifles but confessions in costume, that cruelty may enter by custom before it enters by conviction, and that the self, when pressed by fear, vanity, or indigestion, tells the truth more quickly than philosophy does; so when I find myself offended by a striker’s cowardice in passing backward while I, with heroic discretion, pretend not to see someone from a former committee approaching the bakery, I begin to suspect that my judgments are less moral thunder than weather inside a jar.  

We admire courage most extravagantly from chairs, just as Montaigne’s examples of violence often reveal not grandeur but habit, appetite, and the embarrassing ease with which men convert discomfort into principle; and my own domestic savagery, though limited to the remote control and the phrase “unbelievable,” has the same comic structure as larger barbarities, namely that I demand excellence from bodies I do not inhabit and mercy for the evasions I practice daily under the refined name of temperament.  

The athlete, sweating beneath stadium lights, becomes to me a public instrument for private purification, while the acquaintance, smiling under the awning, becomes a threat to liberty, time, and the fragile republic of my mood; and between these two figures I stand revealed, not as a monster, fortunately, but as the ordinary Montaignian specimen, a creature who mistakes preference for ethics, nerves for judgment, and a loud voice in front of a screen for participation in the world.
